solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: He's often mounted that awful woman on the drink, Brenda

blocks.note: cow is slang for an unpleasant woman
punch is a mixed drink served from a bowl
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose royal cipher is ER

explanation.surface: A rant about a dreadful woman drinking with the Queen, beneath a rider's description.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye always calls the Queen 'Brenda', so she stands for ER, Elizabeth Regina.
explanation.definitionFit: A cowpuncher is an American cowboy, a herdsman who spends much of his working day on horseback.

clue.text: Stunt: one getting head of dick caught in fly

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept
something caught in something else sits inside it, so this pair goes within the outer word

blocks.note: to fly is to flee or escape
one as the article a
first letter of dick

explanation.surface: A cheeky stunt in which something gets caught in a trouser fly.
explanation.walkthrough: The fly is not trousers but the verb to flee; ESCAPE takes A and D inside to make ESCAPADE.
explanation.definitionFit: An escapade is a daring or mischievous adventure, which is what a stunt amounts to.

clue.text: Iron 'universal' Lady almost does U-turn, describing outmoded social system

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped
turning right round sends a driver back the way they came, so the trimmed word reads backwards

blocks.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
U is the film-certificate abbreviation for universal
taken as written before trimming

explanation.surface: The Iron Lady, Thatcher, who famously was 'not for turning', almost does a U-turn.
explanation.walkthrough: The Iron Lady is Margaret Thatcher, whose 'The lady's not for turning' speech gives the surface its joke; here iron is just FE.
explanation.definitionFit: Feudal is the adjective for the medieval system of lords, vassals and land held in return for service.

clue.text: Last fling before union get-rich-quick type leads Labour, say?

blocks.note: on the stock market a stag buys new shares hoping to sell them quickly at a profit
Labour is an example of a political party

explanation.surface: A City speculator heading the Labour Party, with a nod to trade-union links.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'union' is marriage, not a trade union; a stag party is the groom's night out before the wedding.
explanation.definitionFit: A stag party is the groom's celebration with male friends just before his wedding, a final night of freedom.

clue.text: Mimic City address before House

blocks.note: EC is the postcode area for the City of London
HO is the standard abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: Someone at a City address imitating somebody in the House of Commons.
explanation.walkthrough: The City is London's financial district, whose postcodes begin EC.
explanation.definitionFit: To echo is to repeat or imitate what another says or does, the verb sense of mimic.

clue.text: Possible period of government that is gripping Tory leader – insect!

indicators.note: a leader comes at the front, so the first letter of the party name is kept
something gripping another holds it inside, so the short phrase wraps round the kept letter

blocks.note: a term of office
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
first letter of Tory

explanation.surface: A spell of Tory government is likened to a pest eating away at the house.
explanation.definitionFit: A termite is a wood-eating social insect, sometimes called a white ant.

clue.text: Tabloid, second to cosy up to Left

blocks.note: s is the abbreviation for second
port is the left side of a ship

explanation.surface: A tabloid paper playing second fiddle by cosying up to the political Left.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sport (Daily or Sunday Sport) was a lurid British tabloid newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sport was the name of a British tabloid newspaper known for outlandish stories, so the title is an example of a tabloid.

clue.text: Less cloying than "Squidgy", but not as pure as the driven snow?

definitions.text: Less cloying than "Squidgy", but not as pure as the driven snow?

blocks.note: surface reading: the famous Squidgy tapes of Princess Diana's phone calls, gushing romance

blocks.clueFragment: not as pure as the driven snow
blocks.note: setter's reading: half-melted dirty snow, and also something mawkishly sentimental

explanation.walkthrough: 'Squidgy' was the pet name heard on taped calls involving Princess Diana; the answer means both sentimental and like half-melted snow.
explanation.definitionFit: Slushy means sloppily sentimental and also describes snow turned to dirty, watery slush, so it is neither pure nor quite as soppy.

clue.text: (& 23dn.) Party defector's stage act put on film?

blocks.note: a turn is a performer's act in a variety show
to coat is to cover with a thin film or layer

explanation.surface: A political defector's switch is just a piece of theatre made for the cameras.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' suggests cinema but means a thin layer of something.
explanation.definitionFit: A turncoat is someone who deserts one side or party for the opposing one.

clue.text: Two thirds of Boris's former title, "Conservative Live Wire", finally a laughing-stock

indicators.note: taking two thirds of a word means the last third of its letters is thrown away
finally points at the last letter of the word just before it

blocks.note: Boris Johnson once edited The Spectator magazine
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
L marks the live wire in electrical wiring
last letter of wire

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson, once a Conservative live wire, finally becomes a laughing-stock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Title' means a publication: Johnson edited The Spectator before becoming an MP.
explanation.definitionFit: To make a spectacle of yourself is to become an object of ridicule, so a spectacle can be a figure of fun.

clue.text: "Superior", "hard" Murray lacks finish – advantage!

indicators.note: lacking a finish means the name loses its closing letter

blocks.note: upper as in higher in rank
H is the pencil-grading abbreviation for hard
Andy Murray, the Scottish tennis player

explanation.surface: A tennis commentary: a superior, hard-hitting Murray who fails to finish, then 'Advantage!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Advantage' is called in tennis scoring, which fits the Andy Murray surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper hand is a position of control or superiority over a rival, an idiom for advantage.

clue.text: Gordon's chief spin machine alternative? Despondency

indicators.note: the chief letter is the one at the head of the name

blocks.note: first letter of Gordon
a loom weaves yarn rather than spinning it, a different textile machine

explanation.surface: Gordon Brown's chief spin doctor's machine replaced by something else, amid despondency.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spin machine' suggests political spin under Gordon Brown; here it is a textile machine.
explanation.definitionFit: Gloom is a state of low spirits and hopelessness, a synonym for despondency.

clue.text: (& 13ac.) MPs collectively suspended? Electorate could make it happen!

definitions.note: a whole-sentence definition describing the outcome rather than a noun phrase

blocks.note: hung means hanging, suspended
the body of all MPs together is Parliament

explanation.surface: A fantasy of every MP being suspended at once, which voters might bring about.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay reads suspended MPs literally; the definition is the election result in which voters give no party an overall majority.
explanation.definitionFit: A hung parliament results when voters return no single party with an overall majority of seats.

clue.text: see 12ac.
Poser Dave, rubbished by Sun, is a bugger?

indicators.note: something rubbished is trashed and knocked about, so the letters are thrown into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
S is the abbreviation for sun (and Sunday)

explanation.surface: David Cameron, a poser, is trashed by The Sun newspaper, then called a bugger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bugger' looks like an insult but means one who plants listening devices; the Sun is just S.
explanation.definitionFit: To bug is to listen in secretly, so someone who is a bugger is a person who eavesdrops on others' conversations.

clue.text: Daily Mail, etc. balls up takes year to smooth out

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: balls is slang for nonsense, as is rot
y is the abbreviation for year
to press clothes is to iron out creases

explanation.surface: The Daily Mail makes a mess of things and takes a year to tidy it up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Balls up' looks like a single phrase meaning blunder, but balls means nonsense and up flips it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tory press means the Conservative-supporting newspapers, of which the Daily Mail is a prime example.

clue.text: "North's awful", Newcastle ultimately beneath Brenda?

indicators.note: something awful is in a dreadful state, so the letters are messed up
ultimately points at the final letter of the place name

blocks.note: taken as written
last letter of Newcastle

explanation.surface: A northerner's grumble that Newcastle ranks beneath the Queen in importance.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's name for the Queen; the definition is what she sits on.
explanation.definitionFit: A throne is the ceremonial seat of a monarch, so it is literally underneath the Queen when she is enthroned.

clue.text: Cyclops has almost entered election as a sacred offering

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the final letter goes
to have entered something is to be inside it

blocks.note: a vote is an election or ballot
the setter Cyclops speaking of himself: I have, shortened to I've

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of standing in an election as though it were a holy offering.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter's own name stands for I or ME, so 'Cyclops has' is I'VE, cut to IV.
explanation.definitionFit: Votive describes something offered in fulfilment of a vow, such as a candle or gift at a shrine.

clue.text: "If I die" broadcast with 5 Live slated

indicators.note: broadcast also means scattered widely, as seed is, so the letters are spread into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
V is the Roman numeral for five
L is the electrical abbreviation for live

explanation.surface: A programme called 'If I Die' broadcast on BBC Radio 5 Live gets panned.
explanation.walkthrough: Radio 5 Live is a BBC news and sport station; here it is split into V and L.
explanation.definitionFit: To be vilified is to be spoken of with abuse and contempt, much as a show that is slated is harshly criticised.

clue.text: Penny might come first while being penetrated by good bloke

indicators.note: a thing penetrated has something pushed inside it, so the second piece goes within the first

blocks.note: taken as written
a saint is a good person, abbreviated St

explanation.surface: A saucy line about a woman named Penny and a decent chap, with a double meaning.
explanation.walkthrough: Penny is not a woman's name: a penny whistle is a cheap tin flute.
explanation.definitionFit: A penny whistle is a simple six-holed flute, so penny is a word that can precede this answer.

clue.text: Bust, arse wobbles about right with time

indicators.note: something that wobbles is unsteady and out of shape, so its letters are rearranged
about means around, so the rearranged word wraps the following letter

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the abbreviation for right
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A comic picture of bust and backside wobbling about together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like the chest beside 'arse', but it is police slang for an arrest.
explanation.definitionFit: To bust someone is slang for arresting them, as in a drugs bust.

clue.text: Liz, dropping an 'e', on the large side in bustle

indicators.note: dropping a letter means the named letter is removed from the surname

blocks.note: Elizabeth Hurley, the model and actress
burly means big and heavily built

explanation.surface: Liz Hurley, looking rather large, caught in a bustle of activity.
explanation.walkthrough: Liz here is Elizabeth Hurley rather than the Queen, who is Brenda elsewhere in this puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: Hurly-burly is noisy commotion and busy activity, a synonym for bustle.

clue.text: "More work" I pout, when screwed by one

indicators.note: something screwed is twisted, so the letters are twisted into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
one as the article a

explanation.surface: An overworked employee sulks at being asked for more work, with a ruder undertone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'More work' is not extra labour: it means a book by Sir Thomas More.
explanation.definitionFit: Utopia is the 1516 book by Sir Thomas More describing an ideal island society, so it is a More work.

clue.text: Sailor gobbles second powerful person

indicators.note: something gobbled ends up inside the eater, so the second piece goes within the first

blocks.note: tar is an old word for a sailor
s is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: A greedy sailor wolfs down the second helping, like a powerful figure.
explanation.definitionFit: A tsar was the Russian emperor, and the word now means any figure with great authority over an area.

clue.text: see 8dn.
He'd not be slow to fire Darling!

definitions.text: He'd not be slow to fire

blocks.clueFragment: He'd not be slow to fire
blocks.note: first meaning: Alan ..., the businessman famous for 'You're fired!' on The Apprentice
second meaning: a term of endearment

explanation.walkthrough: Darling suggests Alistair Darling, then Chancellor, fitting the political surface; it is really the pet name. Lord Sugar hosted the British version of The Apprentice.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Sugar dismissed contestants with 'You're fired!', and sugar is an affectionate term like honey or sweetheart.

clue.text: (& 28ac.) Over the hill half of Tory leadership overturned – a shadow of its former self

definitions.text: a shadow of its former self

indicators.note: half of a word keeps only its first two of four letters
overturned means flipped over, so the word reads backwards

blocks.note: past one's best, finished
taken as written before halving
the top is the leading position

explanation.surface: A Tory party past its best, its leadership in turmoil, a shadow of itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Something gone to pot has deteriorated badly through neglect, an idiom for being much worse than it was.

clue.text: Dicky (Conservative) turned sour: start of election not going to plan

indicators.note: something turned has gone off and changed, so its letters are rearranged
the start of a word is its first letter, which alone is kept

blocks.note: dicky is British slang for unwell or unreliable, as is off
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
taken as written
first letter of election

explanation.surface: A Conservative called Dicky goes sour as the election campaign goes wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Dicky looks like a name but is British slang for shaky or unwell.
explanation.definitionFit: Off course means having strayed from the intended route, so things are not going to plan.

clue.text: A slimy descent not in the offing for Labour this time?

definitions.text: not in the offing for Labour this time?

blocks.note: first meaning: a mass of earth and mud sliding down a slope

blocks.clueFragment: not in the offing for Labour this time?
blocks.note: second meaning: an overwhelming election victory, unlikely for Labour this time

explanation.walkthrough: Labour won landslide victories in 1997 and 2001; by 2010 such a win looked out of reach.
explanation.definitionFit: A landslide is both a fall of earth and rock down a hillside and a crushing majority in an election.

clue.text: see 25dn.
